section.title: Answer Me When I Call
section.sectionRationale: An evening companion to Psalm 3's morning cry, a lament that turns to instruct doubters before closing in the Psalter's classic image of peaceful sleep under God's care alone.
section.thesis: David asks God to answer his prayer, calls those who chase empty lies to consider their hearts and be still, and finds a joy and peace in the LORD greater than any harvest, sufficient to let him sleep in safety.
section.frameNote: Three movements marked by Selah: the opening plea and rebuke of the honor-seeking crowd (vv1-2), a call to search the heart and trust the LORD (vv3-5), and the closing contrast between empty longing and God-given joy and peace (vv6-8).

units.label: Answer me, and hear the doubters
units.note: how long will you love vanity

verses.text: Answer me when I call, O God of my righteousness! You have relieved my distress; show me grace and hear my prayer.
How long, O men, will my honor be maligned? How long will you love vanity and seek after lies? {{selah|Selah}}

units.label: Be still before the LORD
units.note: the LORD has set apart the godly

verses.text: Know that the LORD has set apart the godly for Himself; the LORD hears when I call to Him.
Be angry, yet do not sin; on your bed, search your heart and be still. {{selah|Selah}}
Offer the sacrifices of the righteous and trust in the LORD.

units.label: Joy, peace, and sleep
units.note: You alone make me dwell in safety

verses.text: Many ask, "Who can show us the good?" Shine the light of Your face upon us, O LORD.
You have filled my heart with more joy than when grain and new wine abound.
I will lie down and sleep in peace, for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety.

selah.gloss: A pause or lifting marker, likely musical or liturgical, inviting the singer to let a truth settle before moving on. Here it falls after the rebuke of the honor-seeking crowd and after the call to search the heart in silence.

basic.context: Psalm 4 is often read as an evening prayer paired with Psalm 3's morning cry. David asks God to answer him as He has before, confronts those who chase empty honor and lies, calls everyone to search their hearts quietly rather than sin in anger, and closes with joy and peace sufficient to sleep safely.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm mixes address to God with direct address to people, a reminder that psalms are not only private prayers but also public instruction; the call to be angry yet not sin anticipates and is later quoted by Paul, Ephesians 4:26, showing the Psalms shaping New Testament ethics directly.
basic.originalLanguages: Twice marked by selah, the psalm pauses first after rebuking those who love vanity and lies, then after urging silence and self-examination on one's bed. The peace of verse 8 uses the rich Hebrew shalom, wholeness, not merely absence of conflict.
basic.typology: David's confidence that God alone makes him dwell in safety, sufficient for untroubled sleep even amid slander, anticipates Christ, who slept in the storm, Mark 4:38, and who is Himself the believer's peace and safety.
basic.christ: Jesus is the ultimate answer to 'who can show us the good'; He is the light of God's face shone upon His people, and in Him believers find a joy greater than any harvest and a peace the world cannot give, John 14:27.
basic.god: God is the one who has already relieved distress before, and is asked to do so again, gracious and near enough to fill the heart with joy exceeding any material abundance, and steady enough to make His people sleep in safety.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 4:26 quotes verse 4 directly, be angry and do not sin. Numbers 6:25 uses the same language of God's face shining. Mark 4:38-39 shows Jesus asleep in peace amid a storm His disciples feared would kill them.
basic.oneStory: Psalm 4 teaches that real distress, real slander, and real anger can be brought honestly to God and answered with a peace deeper than circumstances, a peace fully embodied in Jesus, who is Himself the good that every searching heart asks God to show.

context.literary:
The psalm has the shape of a conversation that keeps changing partners. Verse 1 is spoken to God. Verses 2 to 5 turn to people, first with two sharp questions and then with a run of commands: know, be angry, search, be still, offer, trust. Verse 6 begins with what "many" are saying and slips back into prayer, and verses 7 and 8 close in confession to the LORD. The psalm is a lament that has been overheard by the very people it addresses.

The commands in the middle are the psalm's center of gravity. They are ordered like a small course in spiritual discipline. First, know that the LORD has set apart the godly and hears. Then, in the night, be stirred but do not sin, and hold your tongue. Then offer the sacrifices of the righteous. Then trust. The order moves from knowledge, to the inner life, to worship, to trust, and each step is only possible because of the one before.

The psalm is also built around honor and gladness. "My honor" in verse 2 is the same word as "my glory" in Psalm 3:3, so the two psalms speak to each other. In Psalm 3 David says the LORD is his glory; in Psalm 4 men are dishonoring it. The final verses answer with a better honor, a heart filled with joy that is larger than the joy of a full harvest, and a night's rest that no honor can give.

The beginning and end frame the psalm in a way that is easy to miss. It opens with "Answer me when I call" and ends in sleep, so it moves from an unanswered-sounding cry to a rest that shows the answer has been given. The two selahs sit inside the middle, after the rebuke and after the call to stillness, and they put the weight on the two things the crowd most needs to hear.
context.historical:
The title tells us this song was handed to the choirmaster, to be sung with stringed instruments, so it was written for public worship, not just private prayer. That matches its inward turn: the words to the crowd are meant to be sung in the hearing of the assembly, as the people themselves are addressed. The psalm carries no story in its title, and so we should not force one on it. It may come from the same troubled season of David's life as Psalm 3, and many have read it that way, but the text itself supplies only a man whose honor is attacked and who has known distress before.

The world of the psalm is an agricultural one. Grain and new wine were the two great signs of a good year, and Israel's prophets and lawgivers tie them to the covenant blessing, as Moses does in speaking of a land of grain and new wine, Deuteronomy 33:28. When the psalm says that the LORD has given a joy greater than that of abundant grain and wine, it puts the LORD's gift above the gift that everyone in an agrarian country counted as the mark of a blessed life.

The question of verse 6, "Who can show us the good?" may reflect a hard season in which crops were short and confidence was low. It may also reflect the way that people in any age hunger for evidence of blessing. Nothing in the text settles which. What is clear is that David's opponents were people of some standing who cared about reputation and were ready to spread false stories, and that David's answer was not a counter-campaign but a night's sleep. The picture of a man lying down in safety would have carried weight with a people who knew what it was to sleep with a watch on the walls.
context.canonical:
Psalm 4 quietly draws on the priestly blessing of Numbers 6, in which the LORD is asked to bless and keep His people, to make His face shine on them and be gracious, and to lift up His countenance and give them peace, Numbers 6:24-26. David's prayer that the light of the LORD's face would be upon them, and his closing word of peace, are that blessing in the mouth of one person in need. The blessing was meant to be spoken over Israel; here it becomes a personal prayer.

The theme of sleep given by God runs across the wisdom books. Moses promises that in the land the people will lie down with nothing to fear, Leviticus 26:6. Proverbs says that when you lie down you will not be afraid, and your sleep will be sweet, Proverbs 3:24. Psalm 127:2 says that God gives sleep to His beloved. Peter sleeps in prison the night before his trial, Acts 12:6, and Jesus sleeps on a cushion in the stern in a storm, Mark 4:38.

Paul quotes verse 4 in Ephesians 4:26, "Be angry, yet do not sin," and adds a practical rule that the sun should not set on the anger, and warns against giving the devil a foothold, Ephesians 4:26-27. He is reading the psalm through the Greek Old Testament, and he takes its instruction on how to handle anger and applies it to life in the church.

Jesus' language of peace in John 14:27, "Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you," picks up the closing theme, and Paul promises the peace of God that guards hearts and minds in Christ Jesus, Philippians 4:7. The psalm's last word, safety in the LORD alone, is repeated in the New Testament as the peace that Christ gives.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David meant this psalm to do two things: to teach people how to pray in distress, and to speak to the people who were causing it. Not many psalms address the opponents at length. This one does, because the aim is not only the sufferer's relief but the change of heart in those who love lies. He does not curse them. He asks them a question, "How long?", commands them to reflect, and invites them to trust the LORD.

He also wanted to answer the anxious question of verse 6. When many ask who will show them the good, the psalm's answer is that the good is the face of God and the joy He puts in the heart. A worshipper was to learn that the fullest gifts do not come by success or by the crowd's approval, and they do not disappear when those go.

The final image is for the person lying awake. The night is the hour when the mind replays every insult, and the psalm ends there, by the bed, telling the sufferer what he can do with it: lie down and sleep, because the safety is not his own work.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records David's prayer and his address to others, and much of it is instruction by example. The commands to the crowd are real commands, but they are aimed at that crowd. The parts that carry over to us are best held as patterns. The permission to be angry is a description of a fact that anger arises and a directive to keep it from becoming sin, which is the sense that Paul takes in Ephesians 4:26. It is not a licence to nurse a grievance.

The closing claim that David sleeps in peace is a report of his trust on that night, and not a guarantee of restful nights for every believer. Some of God's people suffer from insomnia, or grief, or illness that no faith removes. The psalm does not condemn them; it points to the underlying safety that stays true when the sleep does not come. In the same way, the joy greater than harvest is not a rule that the godly may not enjoy grain and wine. The Bible celebrates both. It is a claim about which gift is greater.

debates.question: Who are the men addressed in verse 2?

views.label: David's political opponents
views.case: The phrase about maligning his honor and loving lies fits the campaign of slander against a king, and many connect it with the time of Absalom's revolt. On this reading David turns from God to his critics to warn them.

views.label: Wavering members of his own people
views.case: Others think the psalm speaks to Israelites who were drifting toward idols or false hopes, since the word for 'lies' may include false gods and the commands to offer the sacrifices of the righteous and to trust the LORD suit worshippers who needed correcting.

views.label: A general audience of the doubting
views.case: A third view holds that David does not name one group at all. The psalm, in its worship setting, speaks to anyone who is asking the question of verse 6, so that the addressees widen to include the congregation.

debates.bearing: The psalm's commands, know, search, be still, trust, are useful to a person in any of these groups, so the application does not depend on solving the identity.

debates.question: What does 'be angry' mean in verse 4?

views.label: Be angry, but do not sin
views.case: The Greek Old Testament reads it as a command to be angry and yet not sin, and Paul quotes it that way in Ephesians 4:26. On this view the psalm allows righteous anger and puts a limit on it.

views.label: Tremble or be in awe
views.case: The Hebrew verb can mean to quiver or be agitated, whether by rage or by fear, so some translators take the sense to be 'tremble' before the LORD, that is, take the matter seriously, and do not sin.

views.label: Be stirred, and then be still
views.case: A third reading emphasises the sequence: whatever the agitation is, take it to your bed, search the heart and be still. The verbs that follow define the response.

debates.bearing: All three readings warn against acting on agitation in the moment, and Paul's use in Ephesians is faithful to that concern.

study.originalLanguages:
The opening prayer calls God "the God of my righteousness," elohe tsidqi. It means the God who vindicates me, who declares me in the right, and the phrase makes God, not David's reputation, the guarantor of his standing. It is a good answer to the crowd of verse 2, who are attacking his honor. The next line has a beautiful verb: "You have relieved my distress" is literally that in the tight place You gave me room, from the root that means wide, rachav. God's answer to being cornered is space.

In verse 2, the BSB has "O men," and the Hebrew is bene ish, literally sons of man, in a form that often addresses people of some standing. The two charges are "love vanity," reyq, something empty, and "seek after lies," kazav, something false. The verbs are love and seek, the verbs of appetite. The problem is not simply what they say but what they want.

Verse 3 says the LORD has "set apart" the godly, from the verb pala, to make distinct or wonderful. The godly one is chasid, a person of chesed, the loyal faithful love that is the LORD's own character. The one who is loyal to the covenant has been marked out as His own, and so David's prayer is heard.

The commands of verse 4 need attention. "Be angry" is rigzu, which may be to rage or to tremble, and the Greek Old Testament renders it with the verb for anger, as Paul does in Ephesians. "Search your heart" is literally "speak in your heart," imru bilvavkhem, and the picture is of talking to yourself in the dark. "Be still" is dommu, be silent, the verb of hushing. The sequence is a person who is stirred, speaks to himself alone in bed, and then stops talking.

The prayer of verse 6 asks the LORD to "shine the light of Your face." The verb in Hebrew is "lift up," and it carries the same sense as the phrase in the priestly blessing, where the LORD lifts up His countenance and gives peace, Numbers 6:26. The two blessings, shining and lifting, are joined in David's single request. Seeing the face of God is the psalm's answer to "who will show us the good."

Verse 8 uses the word betach for safety, the state of one who is not afraid, and the word yachdav, which can mean "together" or "at once," so the sense may be that lying down and sleeping happen together, in a single motion of trust. The word levadad, "alone," is ambiguous. It can go with the LORD, "You alone make me dwell in safety," or with David, "You make me dwell alone in safety." Both readings are grammatical, and both are true to the psalm.

typology.fulfillment: Jesus sleeping on a cushion in the stern while the storm broke, Mark 4:38, is the psalm lived out. David lay down in peace because the LORD alone made him dwell in safety; Jesus slept in the boat because the Father held Him and because He was Lord of the storm, and the same voice that quieted the sea says peace to His people, Mark 4:39. The escalation is that He is not only kept safe but is the source of the safety. The type falls short because David's sleep was a personal trust, while Christ's rest is the authority that calms the world.

typology.type: The light of the LORD's face, Psalm 4:6
typology.fulfillment: The priestly blessing asked that the LORD's face shine on His people, Numbers 6:25. In the incarnation that face is seen: God who said 'Let light shine out of darkness' made His light shine in our hearts to give the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, 2 Corinthians 4:6. The light David asked for is a person. The correspondence is of the shining face; the escalation is that the light becomes flesh and is given to all who look to Him. The type falls short because the blessing was spoken over the people from outside, while in Christ the light comes to live within them.

typology.type: The sacrifices of the righteous, Psalm 4:5
typology.fulfillment: David commands the offering of the sacrifices of the righteous, which are offerings brought in a right spirit rather than a mere ritual. They point to the one sacrifice that makes people righteous, Hebrews 10:10-14, and to the response of believers who now offer their bodies as a living sacrifice, Romans 12:1. The escalation is from many offerings that had to be repeated to one that is finished. The type falls short in that the old sacrifices could not by themselves cleanse the conscience, while Christ's blood does, Hebrews 9:14.

study.christ:
The psalm asks the question that Christ answers. "Who can show us the good?" is not a question the Old Testament could settle by itself. The best it could do was to point to the face of the LORD and ask that it shine. In Jesus, Paul says, the light of the knowledge of the glory of God is seen in the face of Christ, 2 Corinthians 4:6, and John says the true Light who gives light to every man came into the world, John 1:9. The good that David longed for is a person who has come and can be found.

The peace of verse 8 is His as well. Jesus says, "Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives," John 14:27. The sleep of the psalm has its perfect example in the Lord asleep in the stern of the boat, Mark 4:38, and its perfect explanation in the fact that the one who slept could also say "Be still" to the sea, Mark 4:39. The safety in the psalm is not sheer luck. It flows from the nature of the one who keeps his people.

The invitation to the doubters also finds its center in Christ. "Offer the sacrifices of the righteous and trust in the LORD" becomes, in the New Testament, a call to trust in the one sacrifice that makes us righteous, Hebrews 10:10-14, and to offer ourselves as a living sacrifice in response, Romans 12:1. The call to be still and search the heart is the same call Jesus makes when He says, "Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest," Matthew 11:28.

The parallels here should be held loosely. The psalm is David's, and it should not be forced into a hidden speech of Jesus in every line. But the hunger of the psalm is exactly the hunger the gospel meets, and its answers, the shining face, the joy that exceeds harvest and the safe night, are given in the fullest form in Christ.
study.god:
The God of Psalm 4 is a God who makes room. The first verse says He has done it before, when David was in a tight place, and the request is that He would do it again. It is a picture of God as one whose character is known by past acts: David's confidence rests on what he has seen. The God of the psalm does not need to be persuaded again of His goodness; He is being asked to remain what He has been.

He is a God who sets apart. Verse 3 says the LORD has marked out the godly for Himself, and that is why He hears. The covenant is personal here. God's hearing of prayer is not random but flows from His choice of a people, so that prayer is not an attempt to reach a distant deity but a call to someone who has already claimed us.

He is a God who searches and quiets. The commands of verse 4 assume that the LORD is present at the bedside, in the silence, where the heart is examined. The stillness is not an emptiness; it is a waiting on One who is there. The picture matches Psalm 46:10, "Be still and know that I am God."

He is a God who gives joy. Verse 7 says He has put gladness in the heart, and it is more than what grain and wine can provide. The doctrine of God here refuses to treat joy as a byproduct of circumstances. The LORD is the source of gladness, and the gift is greater than the harvest. It leaves room for both, since the same Bible celebrates the harvest; it simply puts the giver above the gift.

He is a God who keeps. The last verse ties safety to Him alone, and the phrase can be heard two ways. He alone is the source of safety, and He may also be the one who sets a person apart, so that the worshipper dwells safely, alone with his God. For worship, this means the psalm gives a bed-time prayer with a whole theology in it: the character of God, the freedom to be honest about anger, and rest in His care.

crossReferences.note: The priestly blessing asks the LORD to make His face shine on His people, to be gracious, and to give peace. Psalm 4 is a personal use of this blessing, with grace in verse 1, the shining face in verse 6, and peace in verse 8.

Paul quotes 'Be angry, yet do not sin' and adds that the sun should not set on the anger and that the devil should get no foothold. It shows how the church took the psalm's command to handle anger at the bed's edge as a rule for daily life.

In vain do people rise early and stay up late toiling for bread, for God gives sleep to His beloved. It shares the theme of sleep as gift, and it explains why David can lie down: the watchman he trusts is the LORD.

In the covenant promise the LORD gives peace to the land, and the people will lie down with nothing to fear. David's safe sleep in verse 8 is the fulfilment in one person of what was pledged to the whole nation.
When you lie down, you will not be afraid, and your sleep will be sweet. The wisdom writer gives the general rule of a life lived under God that the psalmist here experiences.
Israel dwells securely in a land of grain and new wine. It is the same pair as in Psalm 4:7 and links the joy of the psalm with the covenant blessing, then sets God's gift of gladness above it.
The LORD says, 'Be still and know that I am God.' It gives the same command as Psalm 4:4, be still, and shows the ground for it: stillness is possible because God is God.
Jesus sleeps on the cushion in the stern of the boat and then stills the storm with a word. It is the sleep of Psalm 4:8 in the flesh, together with the authority that makes such sleep safe.
Jesus leaves His peace, not as the world gives. It answers the search of the psalm for a good that does not depend on grain and wine, and it names the giver of the peace of verse 8.

God has made His light shine in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. It is the answer to David's prayer for the light of the LORD's face, given in a person.

The peace of God, which surpasses understanding, will guard hearts and minds in Christ Jesus. It describes the peace of Psalm 4:8 as a guard set over the inner life, so that a heart kept by Christ can lie down as David did.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 4 takes up the question that runs beneath the whole Bible from Eden onward: where is the good to be found? In Genesis 3 the woman saw that the tree was good for food and desirable, and reached for a good apart from God's word. Humanity has been asking ever since, "Who can show us the good?" and many have answered with grain and new wine, honor, and the approval of the crowd. The psalm gives the alternative that the covenant people were meant to hold: the light of the LORD's face, and a heart filled with His joy.

It is also a psalm about the after-effects of the fall on the human interior. Anger, lying, slander and sleeplessness are all fruits of a world where trust has been broken. The psalm does not pretend that they are unreal. It shows them being brought into the presence of God, put to bed, and quieted.

The rest of Scripture builds on this. The Old Testament longs for a peace that is more than the absence of war, the shalom of a restored creation, and the prophets promise that the people will lie down and none will make them afraid. The gospel shows the source of that peace in the one who says He gives it. His resurrection is the beginning of the new order in which sleep is no longer a last defense against the night but a foretaste of the rest to come.

The end of the story is a city where the LORD is the light, and there is no night, Revelation 22:5. There the face of God is seen, and Psalm 17 receives its answer: when I awake I will behold Your face and be satisfied. The prayer for the shining face is answered in full, the question about the good is settled, and the people of God lie down in safety, for He alone has made them dwell there.

sermon.title: Now I Lay Me Down to Sleep
sermon.why: Begg preaches through Psalm 4:1-8, showing that the cry of the heart in its resting moments must be for the vindication of God's glory, and how a softened heart engages the world with compassion and renewed prayer.

quiz.q: What does David ask God to do at the start of Psalm 4?

options.text: Answer him when he calls, show him grace, and hear his prayer, as God has relieved his distress before.
options.note: This opening plea rests on God's past faithfulness as grounds for present confidence.

options.text: Punish his enemies immediately without any prayer for himself.
options.note: The psalm opens with personal petition to God, not primarily a demand for punishment on others.

options.text: Explain why he is suffering.
options.note: David does not ask for an explanation of suffering; he asks God to answer, show grace, and hear him.

options.text: Nothing; the psalm opens with praise only.
options.note: Verse 1 is a direct, urgent petition, not opening praise.

quiz.q: What does David tell the honor-seeking crowd to do in verse 4?

options.text: Be angry, yet not sin, and search their hearts quietly on their beds.
options.note: This instruction is later quoted directly by Paul in Ephesians 4:26.

options.text: Take revenge on those who maligned his honor.
options.note: The psalm calls for self-examination and stillness, not revenge.

options.text: Ignore their anger entirely and suppress all feeling.
options.note: The verse permits anger but calls it toward self-examination rather than sin, not suppression of all feeling.

options.text: Continue chasing vanity and lies without concern.
options.note: This is the opposite of the psalm's instruction, which rebukes exactly this pursuit.

quiz.q: How does David describe the joy God has given him in verse 7?

options.text: Greater than the joy of an abundant harvest of grain and new wine.
options.note: This comparison shows God-given joy exceeding even the greatest material abundance.

options.text: Equal to a modest financial gain.
options.note: The comparison David draws is with abundant harvest joy, a much larger measure than a modest gain.

options.text: Dependent entirely on his outward circumstances improving first.
options.note: The joy described comes from God directly, not from circumstances improving.

options.text: Nonexistent; the psalm ends in despair.
options.note: Verse 7 explicitly describes real, God-given joy, not despair.

quiz.q: What allows David to lie down and sleep in peace in verse 8?

options.text: The LORD alone makes him dwell in safety.
options.note: The verse credits safety and peace entirely to God, not to circumstances or self-reliance.

options.text: His enemies have surrendered.
options.note: The psalm does not describe an external resolution of conflict; the peace is internal trust in God.

options.text: He has secured a strong military guard.
options.note: No military provision is mentioned; the safety described is entirely attributed to the LORD.

options.text: He has forgotten his troubles completely.
options.note: The peace is trust in God amid ongoing distress, not forgetfulness of the trouble.

quiz.q: How does this psalm connect to Jesus?

options.text: Jesus is the light of God's face and the believer's true good, and He slept peacefully in a storm, embodying the same trust that let David sleep amid slander.
options.note: Mark 4:38 shows Jesus asleep in a storm, and John 14:27 shows Him as the source of a peace the world cannot give.

options.text: The psalm has no connection to Jesus or the New Testament.
options.note: Ephesians 4:26 directly quotes this psalm, and its themes of peace and God's face connect clearly to Christ.

options.text: It only describes an Old Testament ritual with no lasting significance.
options.note: The psalm's themes of peace, joy, and God's face carry forward meaningfully into the New Testament's picture of Christ.

options.text: It predicts a specific future event in Jesus' ministry.
options.note: The connection is thematic and typological, not a specific predictive prophecy of an event.

questions: David asks God to answer him again because God has relieved his distress before. What past faithfulness of God can you look back on to fuel your confidence in prayer right now?

David tells the angry crowd to search their hearts quietly on their beds rather than act rashly. When you are angry, what would it look like for you to pause and examine your heart before God rather than react immediately?
David finds a joy greater than any harvest, not tied to his circumstances improving. Where are you currently looking for joy in circumstances rather than in God Himself?

The psalm ends with sleep in peace and safety that comes from the LORD alone, not from David's own security measures. What keeps you awake at night, and what would it mean to entrust that specific worry to God before you sleep?
Jesus slept peacefully in the middle of a storm His disciples feared would kill them. How does His example, and His gift of peace, shape the way you respond to your own storms this week?

translationNotes.note: O God of my righteousness can also be rendered God who vindicates me or God of my right, pointing to God as the one who upholds David's just cause rather than describing David's personal moral righteousness.
Be angry, yet do not sin is quoted directly by Paul in Ephesians 4:26, showing this psalm shaping New Testament ethical instruction almost word for word.
In peace uses the Hebrew shalom, a rich word for wholeness and completeness, not merely the absence of conflict, describing the depth of safety David attributes entirely to the LORD.
